description: How sport supports physical, mental and social health and reduces health risks.
content_html:
What Do We Mean by Health and Wellbeing?

When people talk about being healthy, they often think only about the body — whether someone is fit, slim or free from illness. But health is a much broader concept. The World Health Organization defines health as a state of complete physical, emotional and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. That means a person who is physically fit but socially isolated or constantly anxious is not fully healthy. Understanding all three dimensions of health is essential for explaining how sport and physical activity contribute to a person’s overall wellbeing.

Physical Health

Physical health relates to how well the body functions. Participation in regular physical activity improves physical health in several measurable ways. Cardiovascular fitness improves as the heart becomes stronger and more efficient, lowering resting heart rate and blood pressure. Muscular strength and endurance increase as muscle fibres are recruited and adapted through training. Flexibility improves as joints are taken through a greater range of motion. Body composition shifts as fat mass decreases and lean muscle mass increases. Together, these changes reduce the risk of a range of serious health conditions. Regular physical activity lowers the risk of coronary heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity and osteoporosis. A 35-year-old recreational swimmer who trains three times per week will typically have a lower resting blood pressure, a healthier body weight and stronger bones than a sedentary peer of the same age.

Key Fact

Regular physical activity improves cardiovascular fitness (reducing the risk of coronary heart disease), improves body composition (reducing obesity risk) and increases bone density (reducing the risk of osteoporosis). Each benefit is achieved through specific physiological adaptations during training.

Emotional Health

Emotional health (sometimes called psychological health) refers to a person’s ability to manage feelings and cope with the demands of daily life. Physical activity has a powerful positive effect on emotional wellbeing. Exercise triggers the release of endorphins — natural brain chemicals that create a sense of wellbeing. This is why people often describe a feeling of euphoria after an intense workout or run. Beyond the biochemical effect, regular physical activity has been shown to reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression. It provides a constructive outlet for stress, improves sleep quality and builds confidence as performers see their skills and fitness improve over time.

Sport also provides a sense of purpose, structure and achievement. A teenager who joins a football team has a reason to train, a community to belong to and goals to work towards. Meeting and exceeding personal targets — running a faster mile, scoring a first goal, learning a new gymnastic routine — builds self-esteem. Elite athletes such as Dame Kelly Holmes and Marcus Rashford have spoken publicly about how sport helped them manage mental health challenges, illustrating that the psychological benefits apply at every level of participation.

A common error is to focus only on physical benefits when answering questions about health and wellbeing. Mark schemes reward all three dimensions. For emotional health, a strong answer names the mechanism (endorphin release), the outcome (reduced anxiety/improved mood) and applies it to a realistic scenario. For example: “Taking part in a weekly yoga class reduces cortisol levels and promotes endorphin release, which has been shown to reduce symptoms of mild depression.” Naming the specific benefit and mechanism earns marks; vague phrases like “it makes you feel better” do not.

Social Health

Social health refers to a person’s ability to form and maintain relationships and function within society. Sport and physical activity are uniquely powerful tools for improving social health because they bring people together through shared goals. Team sports such as netball, rugby and basketball require communication, cooperation and mutual trust. Playing together regularly builds friendships, a sense of belonging and social identity. Players who train with the same club for several years often describe the team as a second family.

Beyond team sports, even individual activities carried out in a group context — a running club, a gym class, a swimming squad — provide social contact. This is particularly important for people who are at risk of social isolation, such as older adults or those recovering from injury. Community sport programmes have been used as a public health tool to reduce loneliness and build social cohesion in areas where community bonds have weakened.

Key Fact

Social health benefits of sport include: developing communication and cooperation skills (team sports), building friendships and a sense of belonging (club membership), and reducing social isolation (community sport programmes). Social health improves when sport connects people, not just when it is played.

Positive and Negative Effects of Fitness on Wellbeing

While the benefits of physical activity are well established, it is important to recognise that there can also be negative effects when activity levels are excessive or poorly managed. Overtraining can lead to physical exhaustion, increased injury risk, and — at its most extreme — burnout. Compulsive exercising, sometimes called exercise addiction, can become psychologically harmful if a person feels unable to rest without guilt or anxiety. Pressure to achieve a particular body image through sport can contribute to disordered eating, particularly in sports where weight or aesthetic appearance is judged, such as gymnastics, rowing or wrestling. These negative effects highlight the importance of balance: physical activity should promote wellbeing, not replace one set of health risks with another.

A useful exam technique for 9-mark evaluate questions is to apply all three health dimensions to the same scenario. For example, a 50-year-old who joins a local park run group would gain: physical benefits (improved cardiovascular fitness, reduced blood pressure, healthier weight); emotional benefits (stress relief through endorphin release, improved confidence as times improve); and social benefits (new friendships, sense of community, reduced isolation). A top-band answer evaluates whether these benefits outweigh any risks (overuse injury, time commitment) and reaches a clear, justified conclusion.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain’ questions about health benefits, use the three-step structure: name the benefit, explain the mechanism (how exercise achieves it), and apply it to a sporting example. A common mistake is to confuse physical, emotional and social health — remember: physical = body functions; emotional = feelings and mental state; social = relationships and interaction. For 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions on wellbeing, always include both positive and negative effects, apply each to a sport or athlete, and reach a conclusion that weighs up the balance. One-sided answers that only describe benefits will not reach the top band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health has three dimensions: physical (body function, fitness, disease prevention), emotional (mood, mental wellbeing, stress management) and social (relationships, belonging, community). Sport can improve all three simultaneously.
  • Physical activity reduces health risks including coronary heart disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes and osteoporosis. Endorphin release during exercise underpins many emotional benefits, including reduced anxiety and improved mood.
  • Negative effects are possible with excess or unhealthy engagement — overtraining, exercise addiction and disordered eating can undermine the very health benefits that sport is meant to promote. Balance is essential.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes emotional health?
A) The absence of physical injury
B) The ability to manage feelings and respond to stress constructively
C) The ability to perform sport at a high level
D) The ability to form and maintain relationships
practice_questions.marks: B) The ability to manage feelings and respond to stress constructively [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one physical health benefit and one social health benefit of regular participation in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any physical health benefit, correctly identified (e.g. improved cardiovascular fitness / reduced risk of coronary heart disease / improved body composition / reduced risk of obesity / increased bone density). 1 mark for any social health benefit, correctly identified (e.g. improved communication and cooperation skills / making friends / reduced social isolation / sense of belonging through team membership).

practice_questions.text: Explain how regular participation in sport can improve a person's emotional health.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for naming the mechanism (e.g. exercise triggers endorphin release); 1 mark for explaining the outcome (e.g. endorphins reduce anxiety and improve mood / create a sense of wellbeing); 1 mark for applying to a realistic sporting context (e.g. a swimmer who trains three times per week reports lower stress levels and better sleep quality as a result of the endorphin response during training).

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old joins a local athletics club after a period of low mood and social isolation. Explain how club membership could improve two different dimensions of her health.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for correctly identifying two different health dimensions (e.g. emotional + social). 1 mark each for explaining how the club addresses each dimension. Acceptable content: emotional — structured training goals and achievement of personal bests builds confidence and self-esteem; training triggers endorphin release reducing anxiety; social — training with peers builds friendships and a sense of belonging; shared goals in the team create cooperative bonds that reduce isolation.

practice_questions.text: A club-level cyclist has increased her training volume significantly over the past three months. Analyse the potential positive and negative effects of this increased training on her health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Positive and negative effects discussed across at least two health dimensions; each effect is linked to a specific mechanism (e.g. endorphin release for emotional benefit; overtraining causing fatigue/immune suppression as a negative); consistent application to the cycling context; technically accurate language throughout.

Secure: Both positive and negative effects present; at least two health dimensions touched on; mostly accurate; cycling application present but may be general.

Developing: Either positive or negative effects discussed more fully; limited to one health dimension; some sporting application.

Emerging: Basic list of benefits or risks with little development or sporting application.

Acceptable positive content: improved cardiovascular fitness (reduced coronary heart disease risk); improved body composition; endorphin release improving mood; increased self-confidence as performance improves; social bonds with training partners.
Acceptable negative content: overtraining leading to physical exhaustion, increased injury risk; compulsive training can cause anxiety if rest feels impossible; pressure around body weight/composition in cycling can contribute to disordered eating; social withdrawal if training takes priority over other relationships.

practice_questions.text: A young athlete claims: ‘Sport is always good for your health — there are no downsides.’ Evaluate this statement, considering all three dimensions of health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full discussion across all three health dimensions (physical, emotional, social); balanced argument covering both benefits and risks; consistent sporting application; clear justified conclusion that challenges the athlete’s claim while recognising the genuine benefits.

Secure: At least two dimensions discussed; both benefits and risks present; some sporting application; conclusion present.

Developing: Mainly benefits discussed; limited to one or two dimensions; limited sporting application; argument largely one-sided.

Emerging: Basic list of health benefits with little or no discussion of risks or dimensions.

Agreeing (sport is good): physical benefits (cardiovascular fitness, reduced obesity/CHD/diabetes risk); emotional benefits (endorphin release, reduced anxiety, improved self-esteem); social benefits (teamwork, friendships, community belonging).

Disagreeing / partial challenge: overtraining can cause physical injury, fatigue and immune suppression; exercise addiction can increase anxiety rather than reduce it; social pressure in sport can lead to unhealthy body-image concerns and disordered eating; elite sport demands can isolate athletes from non-sporting social relationships.

Conclusion: Sport is broadly beneficial across all three health dimensions, but the benefits are maximised when training is balanced, goals are healthy, and participation is enjoyable rather than compulsive.

The ability to manage feelings and respond constructively to stress.

Name two physical health benefits of regular exercise.
flashcard_questions.a: Improved cardiovascular fitness and increased bone density.

flashcard_questions.q: How does sport contribute to emotional health beyond endorphin release?
flashcard_questions.a: By building confidence and self-esteem as skills and fitness improve.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might community sport reduce social isolation?
flashcard_questions.a: It provides regular social contact and a sense of belonging for participants.

flashcard_questions.a: Burnout or increased anxiety if rest feels impossible.

flashcard_questions.q: How does regular exercise reduce the risk of osteoporosis?
flashcard_questions.a: By increasing bone density through skeletal loading during training.

flashcard_questions.q: Define 'health' as used in GCSE PE.
flashcard_questions.a: A state of complete physical, emotional and social wellbeing, not merely absence of disease.

glossary_terms.definition: A state of complete physical, emotional and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of disease.
The condition of the body, including how well it functions, its freedom from disease or injury, and its ability to sustain physical demands.
The ability to recognise, understand and manage one's own emotions and respond constructively to stress, anxiety and mental challenges.
Natural chemicals released by the brain during exercise that produce feelings of happiness and reduce the perception of pain.
The ability to form positive, meaningful relationships with others and to interact effectively within society.
A condition characterised by serious disruption of eating habits, often linked to an unhealthy relationship with food and body image.
